## Methods

Nanostructure fabrication and characterization
Both 200-nm nanobar and nanopillar arrays were fabricated via the two-step etching, including optical photolithography followed by reactive ion etching (RIE), as previously reported55. Briefly, quartz wafers were cleaned with Spin Rinse Dryer (SRD), baked, and applied with hexamethyldisilazane (HMDS) to promote photoresist adhesion. The wafers were then coated with a layer of 1-µm-thick photoresist (Shipley 3612) prior to exposure to the desired pattern of UV using Heidelberg (MLA150). The post-exposure wafers were immediately developed with the MF-26A developer (Transene). The AJA e-beam evaporator was subsequently employed to deposit a 120-nm-thick layer of chromium mask on the patterned wafers. After Cr mask deposition, photoresists were immediately lifted off with acetone and isopropanol, and the quartz wafers were etched anisotropically by RIE (Plasma-Therm Versaline LL ICP Dielectric Etcher, PT-Ox) with a mixture of C4F8, H2, and Ar. The quartz wafers were then incubated in 20:1 Buffered oxide etch (BOE) to isotropically shrink nanostructures to the desired dimensions after the removal of the Cr mask with a chromium etchant 1020 (Transene). Nanostructured quartz wafers were then cut into several small chips for cell-based experiments. The shape and dimension of the nanostructures were measured by scanning electron microscopy (FEI Magellan 400 XHR). The SEM imaging was performed once, but across large areas of multiple nanostructured substrates. Detailed dimensions of the nanostructures are described in the main text and figure captions.

Plasmid construction
Wild-type ITGβ5-EGFP (simply noted as ITGβ5-GFP; available from Addgene, #205090) and wild-type ITGβ3-EGFP (noted as ITGβ3-GFP; available from Addgene, #205091) were cloned as previously described40. Briefly, the DNA fragment encoding the human integrin β5 was amplified from the pCX-EGFP β5 integrin receptor (a kind gift from Raymond Birge, Addgene, #14996) using polymerase chain reactions (PCR). The DNA fragment encoding the human integrin β3 was amplified from the complementary DNA (cDNA) of U2OS cells. The fragments were then integrated into the pEGFP-N1 vector (Clontech) through overlap-extension PCR to obtain C-terminally tagged ITGβ5-GFP and ITGβ3-GFP, respectively. All the C-terminally integrin-GFP variants used in this work share a common flexible linker (QSTVPRARDPPVAT), which connects the integrin moiety with GFP.

EGFP-talin-1 (#14996), EGFP-talin-2 (#14996), septin-2-sfGFP (#14996), sfGFP-septin-7 (#14996), and mCherry-tensin-3 (#14996) plasmids were purchased from Addgene. The mCherry-talin-1 plasmid was a kind gift from Michael Davidson (Addgene, #55139), while the mCherry-FCHo2 construct was a kind gift from Christien Merrifield (Addgene, #27686). mCherry-CAAX and FusionRed-CAAX constructs were generated by inserting the DNA fragment encoding the CAAX motif of K-Ras protein (GKKKKKKSKTKCVIM) into the pFusionRed-N vector (Evrogen, #FP412) or the pmCherry-C1 vector (Clontech), respectively.

FCHo2-EGFP, Lyn(SH4)-FCHo2(μHD), and most chimeric ITGβ5/β3-GFP variants were generated via Gibson assembly. Briefly, the linear vector and the fragment were amplified by PCR. Subsequently, the fragment was inserted into the vector and then cyclized in the Gibson Assembly mixture (New England Biolabs, #E2611) composed of 2 U/μL Taq DNA Ligase, 0.025 U/μL Q5 High Fidelity Polymerase, 0.002 U/μL T5 exonuclease, and 0.05 U/μL DpnI at 50°C for 30 min. All truncation variants and mutants of ITGβ5-GFP, ITGβ3-GFP, chimeric ITGβ5/β3-GFP, or mCherry-talin-1 were generated via site-directed mutagenesis with the aid of T4 DNA ligase (New England Biolabs, #M0202). Prior to PCR amplification of fragments for T4 ligation reactions, all primers were subject to 5’-phosphorylation by T4 polynucleotide kinase (PNK, New England Biolabs, #M0201) at 37°C for 30 min. T4 ligation reactions were performed at 37°C for 1 h up to overnight.

All shRNAs (small-hairpin RNA) used in this work were cloned using the protocol from Addgene pLKO.1 Protocol. Briefly, the fragments coding for either scramble shRNA, ITGβ5-shRNA, FCHo2-shRNA, or talin-1/2 shRNA were incorporated into the pLKO.1 vector linearized by AgeI and EcoRI. The gene encoding either BFP (for scramble, FCHo2 shRNA, and talin-1/2 shRNA) or mCherry (for ITGβ5 shRNA) was included in the vector to fluorescently mark the cells that were transiently or stably transfected. Sequence and proposed knockdown efficiency of shRNA are listed in the Supplementary Table 1.

All the oligonucleotides (primers, shRNA-encoding oligos) were purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT).

Substrate functionalization
Substrates were functionalized via a multilayer coating. Nanostructured chips were cleaned in a piranha solution for 2–24 h, then by air plasma for 30–60 min. Cleaned nanostructured chips were placed into a 24-well plate, then coated with 0.2 mg/mL poly-L-lysine (PLL, Sigma-Aldrich, #P5899) for 20–30 min, 0.5% glutaraldehyde (Sigma-Aldrich, #354400) for 20 min, and 25 μg/mL vitronectin (Peprotech, #AF-140-09), fibronectin (Sigma-Aldrich, #F1141) or gelatin (Sigma-Aldrich, #G9391) for 30 min. Subsequently, the chips were incubated with 1X Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, Gibco, #11965092) with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Cytiva, #SH30071) for 30 min to quench free aldehydes. To effectively activate integrin β variants, we used vitronectin as the ECM ligand for the integrin β variants possessing the β5 extracellular domain (i.e., ITGβ5, ITGβ5-5-3, ITGβ5-3-3, ITGβ5-3-5, and x their variants), and fibronectin for those harboring the β3 extracellular domain (i.e., ITGβ3 and its variants, ITGβ3-5-5, and ITGβ3-3-5).

Transient transfection and cell culture
We mainly took advantage of electroporation for transient protein expression. To harvest cells for transfection, confluent U2OS cells (ATCC®, HTB-96TM) were first trypsinized for 5–15 min at 37°C, followed by centrifugation. The pellets were resuspended with 1X DMEM (with 10% FBS but no antibiotics) or 1X PBS. Second centrifugation was applied to remove residual trypsin and EDTA. A half 6-well well of confluent U2OS cells was used for one electroporation reaction. For all ITGβ-and ITGβ3-GFP variants, ~500 ng of plasmid DNA was mixed in a solution composed of 2 μL of electroporation buffer I (360 mM adenosine 5′-triphosphate and 600 mM magnesium chloride) and 100 μL of electroporation buffer II (88 mM monobasic potassium phosphate and 14 mM sodium bicarbonate at pH=7.4). If desired, ~1.5 μg of plasmid DNA encoding either scramble, ITGβ5, or FCHo2 shRNAs were included in the mixture. Cell pellets were gently resuspended with the electroporation mixture and subsequently transferred into a 0.2-cm electroporation cuvette (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #FB102). The cell-DNA mixture was then electroporated with a U2OS-specific program using Amaxa Nucleofector II (Lonza). To complete the electroporation, the mixture was immediately added with 800–1000 μL of pre-warmed (37°C) 1X DMEM (with 10% FBS but no antibiotics) and incubated for 10–15 min. Cells were then harvested by spinning and resuspended with 1X DMEM with 10% FBS, 100 U/mL penicillin and 100 mg/mL streptomycin (Gibco, #15140122). The transfected cells were cultured in a 6-well or 12-well plate, and maintained in a standard incubator at 37°C with 5% CO2 for 72 h.

After 72-h incubation, ITGβ-GFP-transfected U2OS cells were detached from well plates with a pre-warmed 5 mM EDTA in 1X PBS at 37°C for 15–20 min. Cells were then harvested via spinning. If needed, 72-hr-cultured U2OS cells expressing a given ITGβ-GFP variant were further co-transfected with ~500 ng of the constructs for mCherry-FCHo2, mCherry-talin-1, or their variants, via electroporation. After resuspending cell pellets with 1X DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and antibiotics, desired amounts of U2OS cells were then plated on the functionalized nanostructured or flat substrates and maintained in 1X DMEM (with 10% FBS and antibiotics). The cultures were incubated in a standard incubator for 24 h at 37°C with 5% CO2. Upon 96-h incubation (72-h post-transfection incubation plus 24-h plating/culture on substrates), the majority of ITGβ-GFP signals were localized to the plasma membrane and adhesion architectures, with a small residual amount trapped in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or perinuclear regions. Cells exhibiting strong ER-localized ITGβ-GFP signals were excluded from all analyses.

For overexpression of GFP-talin-1, GFP-talin-2, mCherry-tensin-3, septin-2-GFP, GFP-septin-7, or FusionRed-CAAX, 300–400 ng of plasmids were used for electroporation. If integrin β-GFP overexpression was omitted (for instance, endogenous ITGβ5 immunostaining experiments), 24-h post-transfection culture on substrates was sufficient.

Cell membrane visualization
To visualize the plasma membrane in U2OS cells, we mostly performed transient expression of the fluorescent CAAX (FusionRed-CAAX). 72-hr-cultured U2OS cells transfected with a given ITGβ-GFP variant were further co-transfected with ~300 ng of the FusionRed-CAAX plasmid via electroporation. For three-channel imaging, we transiently transfected U2OS cells with an extracellular SNAP-tag to label the plasma membrane with Alexa Fluor 647. Briefly, cells were transfected with SNAP-pDisplay and then incubated in a pre-warmed 1X DMEM medium supplemented with 1 µM O6-benzylguanine (BG)-coupled Alexa Fluor 647 (NEB, #806S9136S) at 37°C with 5% CO2. After 15-min incubation, the samples were washed 5 times with a pre-warmed 1X DMEM medium before fixation and imaging.

Cell fixation and immunostaining
To probe the endogenous ITGβ5, overnight-seeded U2OS cells (on either nanostructured substrates or flat surfaces) were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #28908) in 1X PBS at room temperature for 15 min. To preserve focal adhesion architectures marked by cytoskeletal adapters (i.e., talin-1, talin-2, tensin-3, kindlin, and vinculin), cells were instead fixed in 4% PFA in 1X PHEM buffer (60 mM PIPES, 25 mM HEPES, 10 mM EGTA, 2 mM MgCl2, pH=7.0) at room temperature for 5–10 min. After three washes with 1X PBS, cells were then permeabilized and blocked with 0.1% Triton X-100 and 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA) (Sigma-Aldrich, #A9418) in 1X PBS (staining buffer) at room temperature for 1 h. Cells were then incubated with rabbit anti-ITGβ5 (Cell Signaling, clone D24A5, #3629S), mouse anti-kindlin-2 antibody (Antibodies.com, clone 3A3, #A277536), or mouse anti-vinculin antibody (Sigma-Aldrich, clone hVIN-1, #V9131) at 1:500 dilution in the staining buffer for 0.5-1 h at room temperature. After three washes with 1X PBS, cells were then stained with secondary antibodies (goat anti-rabbit IgG Alexa Fluor 647 (Invitrogen, #A-32733), goat anti-mouse IgG Alexa Fluor 488 (Invitrogen, #A-32723), or goat anti-mouse IgG Alexa Fluor 594 (Invitrogen, #A-11032)) at 1:500 dilution in the staining buffer for 0.5–1 h at room temperature in the dark. Samples were washed with 1X PBS three times prior to fluorescence imaging.

For A549 cell (ATCC®, CCL-185TM) experiments, blank (untreated, wild-type) cells were mixed with FCHo2-depleted ones, then subsequently plated onto vitronectin-coated nanobar arrays or flat substrates. 4 h post plating and prior fluorescence imaging, cells were fixed, permeabilized, and stained with phalloidin (Invitrogen, Alexa Fluor 647-labeled, #A22287), rabbit anti-ITGβ5, and mouse anti-vinculin.

The antibodies used in this work are listed in the Supplementary Table 2.

Mn2+ treatment experiments
Overnight-seeded ITGβ-GFP-expressing U2OS cells were incubated with 0.5 mM Mn(NO3)2 (Supelco, #1.19789) in a pre-warmed DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and antibiotics for 20 min at 37°C. Upon completion of the treatment, cells were washed and fixed prior to imaging.

EDTA treatment experiments
For EDTA treatment experiments, live cell assays were performed. Prior to EDTA addition, overnight-seeded ITGβ-GFP-expressing U2OS cells were first imaged to record before signals. Cells were then treated with 5 mM EDTA (Invitrogen, #15575020) in a pre-warmed DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and antibiotics for 4–5 min at 37°C, and the samples were imaged at 37°C in a microscopic chamber supplemented with 5% CO2 to record after signals.

Lentiviral particle generation for stable shRNA knockdown
We followed and modified the protocol for lentiviral particle generation from Addgene pLKO.1 Protocol. Briefly, HEK293T cells (ATCC®, CRL-3216TM) were cultured in 1X DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and antibiotics in six-well plates to reach ~70–80% confluency. Prior to transient transfection, the growth medium was replaced with pre-warmed opti-MEM. Subsequently, HEK293T cells were transiently transfected with 0.8 µg psPAX2 plasmid, 0.7 µg pMD2.G plasmid, and 1.5 µg transfer plasmid encoding pLKO.1-shRNA-BFP constructs using Lipofectamine 2000. The transfection mixture was replaced with fresh 1X DMEM (with 10% FBS, 1 mM sodium pyruvate (11360; Gibco), and antibiotics) 6 h post-transfection. The virus-containing supernatants were collected and filtered through 0.45-µm polyvinylidene difluoride filters (Millipore) 24–48 h after transfection. Target cells (U2OS or A549 cells) were transduced with lentivirus and incubated for at least 4–72 h prior to fluorescence imaging experiments or Western blot analysis.

Western blot analysis for shRNA knockdown
U2OS cells were transduced with lentivirus harboring shRNA of interest and incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2 for 2–3 days. 24 h post transduction, virus-containing growth medium was removed and replaced with fresh 1X DMEM (with 10% FBS and antibiotics), allowing cells to grow for 1–2 more days (2–3 days in total). Prior to lysis, cells were detached with EDTA, harvested by spinning, and rinsed with ice-cold 1X PBS. The cell pellets were resuspended and lysed in 1X RIPA buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 1% sodium deoxycholate, and 0.1% sodium dodecyl sulfate) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktails (Roche, #04693159001 and #04906837001) for 1 h at 4°C. For probing the endogenous ITGβ5, the samples were further boiled for 10 min at 95°C. The clarified lysates were mixed with 4X Laemmli sample buffer (Bio-Rad, #1610747) and β-mercaptoethanol, and boiled for 5 min at 95°C. The samples were subsequently resolved by SDS-PAGE using Mini-Protean vertical electrophoresis system (Bio-Rad, #1658026FC) for 60-70 min at 100–110 V. After SDS-PAGE, the samples were then transferred onto a nitrocellulose membrane using a Trans-Blot Turbo Transfer system (Bio-Rad, #1704150) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The membranes were blocked with 3% BSA in 1X TBST buffer for 30 min at room temperature and then incubated with primary antibodies (rabbit anti-ITGβ5 (Cell Signaling, clone D24A5, #3629S), rabbit anti-FCHo2 (Novus Biologicals, Polyclonal, #NBP2-32694), or rabbit anti-GAPDH (Cell Signaling, clone 14C10, #2118) overnight at 4°C. After 1-h incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature, the protein bands were visualized through chemiluminescent signals by Azure Imaging Systems (Azure Biosystem).

Fluorescence imaging
Fluorescence imaging was performed using an epi-fluorescence microscope (Leica DMI 8000) controlled by the Leica LAS X Leica LED8 system. Nanostructured chips were flipped and placed on a glass-bottom petri dish when imaging cells55. The samples were imaged with a 63X oil immersion objective (N.A.=1.4) and acquired using the K8 Scientific CMOS microscope camera.

Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) assay
FRAP was performed using a confocal microscope (Nikon A1plus) controlled by NIS-Elements AR. The ITGβ5-GFP signals were imaged with a 488 nm laser using a 63X oil immersion objective (N.A.=1.4). 1-μm-diameter circular ROIs at nanopillars were bleached for 2 s using the 488-nm at ~10% power. Pre-bleaching (−5 to −10 frames) and post-bleaching time courses were acquired at 1 s/frame for around 5 min.

Quantification of normalized nanobar end-to-side intensity ratios
The details and flowchart for the analysis are described in our previous work40,56. Briefly, fluorescence images were processed and analyzed using MATLAB (Version 2021a) and Fiji (ImageJ 2, Version 2.3.0). We use a custom-written MATLAB code to generate a matrix of masks to include each nanobar covered by cells in the bright-field channel. These masks were then applied to the fluorescence channels to create 40*40-pixel averaged images of proteins of interest (POIs) on nanobars. Background subtraction using the rolling ball algorithm with a radius of 1000 pixels was applied to the average images before quantifying nanobar end-to-side ratios. We used a 3*3-pixel square to cover the regions of interest (ROIs) on a nanobar, including nanobar ends and flat side walls (Supplementary Fig. 1C). The nanobar end-to-side intensity ratios from multiple nanobars in an individual cell were averaged and are reported as a single data point. Based on the integrity of nanostructures and the location of a cell adhered to nanostructured substrates, a single cell may cover a wide range of numbers of nanobars from ~30 nanobars/cell to ~300 nanobars/cell.

Quantification of spatial correlation at nanopillars
The details for the analysis are described in our previous work40. To quantify the spatial correlation between two POIs at nanopillar locations, the individual fluorescence images of POIs, rather than the averaged ones, were extracted using the abovementioned custom-written MATLAB code. After background subtraction using the rolling ball algorithm with a radius of 1000 pixels, the nanopillar ROIs were selected by a 7-pixel-diameter circle, and the mean fluorescence intensities of POIs at individual nanopillars were measured using Fiji. The degree of spatial correlation between two arrays of POIs’ intensities at individual nanopillars in a cell, reflected by the Pearson’s correlation coefficients, was calculated using Prism 9 (GraphPad Software). The Pearson’s correlation coefficients measured from each cell are reported as a single data point. Based on the integrity of nanostructures and the location of a cell adhered to nanostructured substrates, a single cell may cover a wide range of numbers of nanopillars from ~60 nanopillars/cell to ~700 nanopillars/cell.

Quantification of normalized nanopillar-to-surrounding intensity ratios
The details and flowchart for the analysis are described in our previous work40,56. The analysis pipeline resembles that for nanobar end-to-side intensity ratio quantifications. The 20*20-pixel averaged images of proteins of interest at nanopillars were background-subtracted. A 7-pixel-diameter circle was then employed to cover the nanopillar ROIs, with the rest of the areas serving as the surrounding ROIs (Supplementary Fig. 6B). The nanopillar-to-surrounding intensity from multiple nanopillars in an individual cell was averaged and reported as a single data point.

Quantification of focal adhesions on flat substrates
We adapted and modified the analysis method for quantifying focal adhesions from a previous work99. All the processes were performed using Fiji. Briefly, the ROIs were first selected using the wand tool. Fluorescence images were background-subtracted by the rolling ball algorithm (radius=25 pixels, sliding paraboloid). Subsequently, we ran the CLAHE plug-in to enhance the local contrast of the images (block size=9, histogram bins=128, maximum slope=6, no mask and no fast), followed by a mathematical exponential (EXP) to further reduce backgrounds. The brightness and contrast of the images were then adjusted automatically, and thresholding was performed using the Huang method. Eventually, we quantified the focal area percentage (Total focal adhesion area per cell area) and the number of focal adhesions per cell through the ANALYZE PARTICLES function (size=0.5–25 μm2, circularity=0.00–0.99, no Exclude on edges).

Statistics and reproducibility
All statistical analyses were performed using Prism 9. Parametric, Welch’s t-tests (unpaired, two-tailed, not assuming equal variance) were employed to evaluate the statistical significance for the quantifications of curvature-related measurements (i.e., normalized nanobar end-to-side intensity ratios, Pearson’s correlation coefficients at nanopillars, etc.), while nonparametric, Mann-Whitney test (unpaired, two-tailed) was used for assessing the statistical difference for the quantifications of focal adhesions (i.e., total focal adhesion area per cell area and number of focal adhesions per cell). Exact P-values are provided in the figures. For the bar graphs, data are presented as mean±SD; for the violin plots, the solid black lines indicate the median. Each data point represents one cell; all the data points from each experimental condition were compiled from at least 2–3 biological replicates to ensure reproducibility. All measurements were taken from distinct samples; no sample was measured repeatedly. No sample size calculation was performed. No data were excluded from all analyses except for cells exhibiting strong ER-localized ITGβ-GFP signals. No data randomization was performed in this work. No blinding was performed in this work; all data were collected automatically by instruments rather than by human evaluation.

Reporting summary
Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Data availability
The numeric values and n values for each experimental condition in this work are provided as a Source Data file. All the results shown in this work are provided in this file. Plasmid constructs generated in the work will be available from the corresponding author upon request. Source data are provided with this paper.

Code availability
The custom MATLAB codes used in this study for quantifications of nanobar- and nanopillar-related experiments (i.e., curved adhesions) were published in our previous research40 and deposited at GitHub (https://github.com/wzhang5publication/Data-analysis). Additional information will be available from the corresponding author upon request.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The authors of the paper presented interesting observations showing that only integrin β5 can be targeted to curved membranes made of artificial nanostructures created by nanobars. The targeting of integrin to the curved membrane was possible due to the β5 Y766 phosphorylation, which reduces talin binding and allows its interaction with the curvature-sensing protein FCHo2. Since β5 is targeted to the curved membrane in an FCHo2-dependent manner and interacts with its ligand, the authors suggest that FCHo2 binding activates integrin αvβ5 at curved membranes. Furthermore, they showed that the β5 transmembrane domain is also important for curved membrane targeting, which requires further investigation. That study would give a helpful insight into the field, if some issues below can be addressed.
1. The authors used nanobars with a height of 1 µm. However, cellular thickness, especially at the peripheral regions, can be less than 1 µm, leading to both inward positive curvature at the basal surface and outward negative curvature at the apical surface from the same nanobar, as shown by the authors in their previous study (PMID: 31591250, Fig 1I). This raises question about whether the fluorescence signals shown throughout the manuscript come solely from positive curvature, as the authors suggest (Fig. 1B), or also from negative curvature positioned above the positive curvature, or from the space between these different curvature types. This ambiguity remains unless the cell thickness in the regions of interest is considered, e.g. by adopting some z-section study.
2. In most experiments, integrin β subunits fused to GFP were transiently transfected, potentially leading to its accumulation in the ER. This makes it unclear whether the fluorescence near the nanobars represents integrins at the cell surface or within the ER or other intracellular organelles. Similarly, it is not clear whether integrin β mutants, especially ITGβ5-3-3(1-755/769) used in Fig. 5J, can actually form integrin αvβ5 complexes on the cell surface and near the nanobars as well.
3. The cell images were taken after 24 hours of plating on vitronectin-coated nanobars, even with the presence of 10% FBS (line 677). To observe the intended interactions between αvβ5 and vitronectin at the nanobars, an incubation of 30 minutes to 1 hour in the absence of FBS would be enough. A 24-hour incubation with FBS could introduce unwanted interactions due to ECM components in the serum or from cells adhering to the surface, allowing various endogenous integrins to engage in cell-substrate interactions. An experiment under a 30-minute to 1-hour FBS-free incubation should be considered, to confirm the results obtained by their 24 hour/FBS method.
4. The main conclusion of the extensive mutation studies in Figs. 1 and 2 is that the phosphorylation state of Y766 determines the localization of β5. Without phosphorylation, β5 binds to talin and is recruited to focal adhesions. When phosphorylated, β5 does not bind talin (or its affinity is reduced) and is recruited to curved membranes. However, there is no direct demonstration of the phosphorylation status of integrin β5. For example, in the sentence on line 252, “Among all the mutants, only the variants with Y766 can form both focal adhesions and curved adhesions, likely due to its dual phosphorylation states,” it is critical to show whether β5 indeed possesses dual phosphorylation states, e.g. by using pY specific antibody of β5 immunoprecipitates or by mass spectroscopy.
5. If the Y766 phosphorylation hypothesis is correct, could the talin-binding-defective β5 Y774A mutant be phosphorylated more than the wild type? Or, could talin overexpression inhibit β5 Y766 phosphorylation? Is there any evidence that “phosphorylation of β5Y766 would abolish the cation-π interaction and drastically alter the interaction” (Line 194)? In addition, could talin knockout lead to the preferential localization of β3 at the curved membrane?
6. The authors suggest that the unique Tyrosine residue in β5 (Y766) is responsible for targeting it to curved membranes, thereby facilitating cell adhesion in 3D ECM fibers or during endocytosis. In contrast, other β integrins, containing tryptophan at the corresponding position, cannot be targeted to curved membranes. Then the question is, do cells not form focal adhesions but only curvature adhesions in 3D ECM fibers? Moreover, other integrins play roles in binding fibrous ECM (e.g., β1 integrins to collagen fibers) and endocytosis (e.g., β2 integrins during phagocytosis), even with the tryptophan residue. This raises questions about the physiological relevance of β5 targeting to curved membranes.
7. Biochemical evidence is required for the hypothesis that talin binding to the MP site prevents FCHo2 binding (line 257). For example, an in vitro experiment using purified integrin β tails (wild type vs. Y766E vs. HDRRE) and FCHo2 interaction in the presence of increasing amounts of purified talin should be performed. Only cell biology experiments is not sufficient to prove the hypothesis.
8. Although the authors concluded that FCHo2 is essential for inside-out activation of ITGβ5 at curved membranes (lines 411 and 452), no mechanistic explanation for the activation is provided. Rather, it seems to me that ITGβ5 binds to the ligand on the curved membrane first for some reasons, e.g. by the curvature itself (PMID: 32634408), and that FCHo2 is recruited to the region due to both the curvature and its binding site in the integrin, which can stabilize the integrin complex as suggested by the authors (line 444). To support the argument that FCHo2 is essential for ITGβ5 activation at curved membranes, it would be important to demonstrate whether FCHo2-bound ITGβ5 (on curved membranes, in the absence of ligand) adopts an active conformation or increases ligand binding, as ligands themselves can also activate integrins (PMID: 38772370).
9. Some minor comments:
- Line 143: Is the end-to-side ratio of ~1.55 significant enough compared to enrichment in focal adhesions?
- Line 144: Focal adhesions formed along the nanobar sidewall are not visible.
- Line 330: “Bridget” -> “bridge”
- Including the exact amino acid sequences near the transmembrane domain of the chimeric integrins (β5-5-3, β5-3-3, β5-3-5, β3-3-5, β3-5-5) shown in Figure 5 would provide more informative detail.

### Reviewer 2

Comments to Lu and co-workers (FCHo2-manuscript) :
This manuscript is a continuation of the initial description of curved adhesion formed by the integrin avb5 on surfaces with positive nanostructures, or fibrous extracellular material (Zhang et al., 2023). In the initial paper, curved adhesion recruited talin and FCHo2, and now the current manuscript aims to better understand the relative recruitment of these two adapter proteins. Thus, the authors analyze how the interplay of talin and FCHo2 is modifying the formation of avb5-containing focal adhesion versus curved adhesions. On flat surfaces, the authors propose that FCHo2 is potentially excluded by Talin-binding to the juxtamembrane (JM) region of b5-integrin, as long as a critical tyrosine residue in the vicinity of the membrane distal NPLY-motif is not-phosphorylated. Upon phosphorylation of this tyrosine, talin binding is potentially reduced, leading to the preferred recruitment of avb5 to curved adhesions. Further mutational analysis of the JM-region in different b5/b3-integrin chimeras proposes that curvature sensing and FCHo2-binding requires a conserved membrane-proximal HDRRE-motif. By performing divalent cation restriction and FCHo2-siRNA treatment, the authors claim that FCHo2 is binding only to activated integrins and is itself involved in inside-out activation of avb5, at these sites. Ultimately, with transmembrane domain swapping experiments the authors propose that the b5-transmembrane domain is also regulating the ability of the avb5 integrin to localize to curved adhesions. The manuscript appears technically sound, describing a potentially new type of focal adhesions formed by avb5 integrins, and its regulation by a new type of curvature-sensing adapter protein. Nevertheless, I would like to propose a few additional experiments, to make sure that the claim by the authors of differential, and competitive binding of talin and FCHo2 to the JM domain of avb5 can be affirmed. Alternatively, a model in which the synergy between talin and FCHo2 leads to the formation of very stable adhesions could be a mechanisms how to explain the extraordinary stability of these curved adhesion (80 min). It would also be very good if the latter proposal of adhesion stability would be confirmed by more quantitative measurements involving fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, or fluorescence activation measurements.
Major issues.
Throughout the manuscript, the authors are comparing talin1 association with that of FCHo2 for the JM domain of avb5. In previous studies in U2OS-cells, talin-1 was excluded from avb5 integrins that participated in reticular adhesions. Instead tensin-3 and talin-2 showed strong co-localization with this particular adhesion type in these cells. It is not yet clear why talin-2 and or tensin-3 show a preference for avb5 in reticular adhesions, and do not co-localize with avb3, the main other integrin used in this study. For completion, it would be really important to inform the readers, whether curved adhesions can recruit both or either one of these adapter proteins. Thus transfection with talin-2 RFP, or tensin-3 GFP would be helpful to identify if these proteins can be recruited to curved adhesions as well.
Furthermore in figure 1, b5-5-3 constructs are used to eliminate talin-1 binding by Y774A-mutation, which then still resulted in curved adhesion recruitment of the latter integrin. In the past it has been shown that equivalent avb3-Y774A mutants can still recruit and co-cluster with the talin-1-head domain when activated with Mn2+ (Saltel et al., 2009, cited). Because of the possible recruitment of talin to the JM-region independent of Y774A, it would be relevant to exclude that not talin-2 is occupying the place vacated by talin-1. As only complete double talin-depletion results in the loss of adhesion, it might well be possible that FCHo2 is still recruited to a JM/talin-head complex in a membrane curvature-dependent manner, but independent of the Y774-residue.
To make sure the reason for FCHo2 exclusion from focal adhesions is not only due to talin competition, but rather a lack of membrane-recruitment, it would be important to exchange the lipid-sensing domain of FCHo2 (F-bar-domain), with that of a relevant PIP2-sensing domain. This would be the appropriate control, in order to affirm that the missing localization of FCHo2 at focal adhesions is due to lack of membrane interaction, as compared to a lack of competition with talin-binding to integrins.
Figure 3: the c-terminal truncation analysis is helpful to see the adhesion phenotype in Fig3 B, and C. However when the point mutations in the HDRRE region are analyzed, this is done in the context of the FL-construct of b5-integrin (panels I-L), favoring the overall talin binding to the cytoplasmic tail. Therefore the sensitivity of the two recruitment assays are not equivalent, the analysis represented in panels I-L should be performed with a truncation mutant (e.g. 1-759), which forms the minimal FCHo2 binding site, with neglectable interference by talin-recruitment.
In the past JM-domain mutations have been performed to characterize the linkage between b3-integrin and talin1-head domain. While certain studies showed relevance of the di-phe-motif for talin/b3-binding, other studies showed an electrostatic interaction between K316 in talin-1 and b3-E726 (E753 in this study), which could be swapped between the two partners (Saltel et al., 2009). While the E753K mutation perturbs curved adhesion formation, and FCHo2 recruitment, the authors could co-express talin-1 (K316E), to rescue the talin-1 binding defect. If this complementation by talin (K316E) is unable to rescue the curved adhesion defect, the authors can clearly claim the independent association of talin-1 and FCHo2. At the current state of the mutagenesis study of the HDRRE-motif, it is not clear whether and how the point-mutations are directly or indirectly affecting the talin-1 interaction in the JM-region (as for example shown for the D750A mutant). Furthermore, as the talin/JM interaction involves only one side of the helical JM-domain, it might well be possible that the other side (e.g. R751 and R752) can be contacted by the adapter protein FCHo2, in a synergistic manner.
Previously, the activation and association of talin with integrin avb3 has been probed with talin-head fragments only, and also modulated by the addition of Mn2+ to keep avb3 in an open conformation. Since avb5 has always been detected in more central cellular locations, (compared to avb3 localized to peripheral adhesions), its basal activation state is likely increased, when compared to avb3. Based on the authors analysis with the chimeric integrins, it appears that the transmembrane domain of b5, has the capacity to shift the conformational equilibrium of the ectodomain to the open conformation, allowing for enhanced outside-in activation of avb5 over avb3. Have the authors attempted to reveal the curved adhesions recruitment of avb3, with Mn2+ treatment (and on vitronectin surfaces)?
When expressed as a full-length protein, talin1 is autoinhibited, and part of its activation mechanisms requires binding to acidic lipids. Truncating the basic residues in the head-domain will actually not fully reveal their potential importance, in the recruitment or activity of integrins in curved adhesions, as the talin protein remains inactiv and hence integrin binding is obscured. In the past, talin1/b3-interaction studies have therefore been performed with the truncated talin head domain, or more recently with a full-length version of talin-1 mutated in the R9-bundle. It would be interesting to see whether dominant active forms of talin-1 or talin-2 (e.g. activate at the autoinhibitory site in the R9-bundle) would be able to perturb recruitment of avb5 to curved adhesions.
Minor issues:
Figure 3: It would be good to indicate the position and sequence of the peptide linkers used for the GFP-fusion constructs in figure 3A.
Figure 5 (but also figure 1). It is not fair to use fibronectin as a ligand for avb3, as this FN-binding requires force for avb3 activation (Bachmann et al., JCS 2020; induction of ligand promiscuity of avb3 by force…). Therefore, the authors should also use vitronectin coating for the analysis of avb3 integrin recruitment to curved adhesion and could then also use relatively easy ways to modulate the activation state of the integrin (e.g. +/- Mn2+).
Figure 5: the b3-5-3 mutant is missing in the analysis, is it equivalent to the b3-5-5? please explain.
Line 556: “cured” should probably read “curved”.

### Reviewer 3

The present study is based on a previous work of the same lab reporting « curvature-dependent integrin-mediated adhesions called curved adhesions » published in Nature Cell Biology in 2022. In this previous paper the authors showed that the curved adhesions recruit integrin ɑvβ5 and talin (but not vinculin and pFAK), bear mechanical forces (but lower than focal adhesions) and are molecularly distinct from focal adhesions and clathrin lattices by involving a a curvature-sensing protein, FCHo2 interacting with integrin β5.
Herein, using the same kind of nanostructure platform to induce well-defined membrane curvatures in live cells, the authors proposes a molecular basis for discriminating focal adhesions from curved adhesions and the exclusive formation of curved adhesions by integrin ɑvβ5. Having previously shown that curved adhesions require the juxtamembrane region of ITGβ5 cytoplasmic tail, the authors designed truncations and mutations at the level of ITGβ5 cytoplasmic tail. They have identified the tyrosine (Y766) as specific residues in β5 tail. This tyrosine is replaced by a tryptophan (W) which is conserved in all homologous integrin β isoforms. The presence of tyrosine Y766 and its phosphorylated state are crucial for the localisation of β5 integrin in curved adhesions while its replacement by the tryptophan residue does not impair β5 integrin localization in focal adhesions. Disrupting the ɑβ salt bridge is not sufficient for the formation of curved adhesions, while FCHo2 binding to the HDRRE region is crucial. Talin is recruited in both focal adhesions and curved adhesions. Talin binding is crucial for integrin activations in focal adhesions but it is dispensable in curved adhesions. In curved adhesions, talin would with HDRRE motif to consequently activate ɑvβ5 integrin independently on talin. The experiments are well designed. However the biological or physiological relevance is missing and should be analyzed a little be further.
As already reported by the same lab, curved adhesions bear mechanical forces.
-Using vertical nanopillars arrays from fig.3D is somehow puzzling. Does it mean that some conditions are not working with previous nanobars?
-Is the engagement of talin to only MD site sufficient to induce force generation (even low) in curved adhesions ? How are these forces generated ? If FCHo2 is an alternative to talin, capable of inducing inside-out integrin activations selectively at curved membranes, what are the consequences on myosin and actin in the model of curved adhesions ? Do we expect any change of actin organization, myosin distribution or even force dysregulation ? All the mutants designed in this study are available to perform experiments related to actin and force regulation and give an answer about actin/myosin based force in curved adhesion.
-In case of non-involvement of actin, one can consider septin giving the septin-bundling activity of FCHo2 (PMID: 36476870).
-In addition, Tensin shares the same binding site as talin includind W residues (see Legate and Fassler, JCS PMID: 19118211) and they can be mutually exclusive. Moreover, keratin network is as an integral part of force-sensing elements recruiting distinct proteins like tensin (PMID: 31527270; PMCID). Is tensin (and possibly keratin) an alternative to talin (and actin) by working in concert with FCHo2 ? This would greatly complete this study to better discriminate curved adhesions from focal adhesions and to identify an alternative for force generation involving FCHo2 and not talin.
Knowing that curved adhesions facilitate cell migration in 3D ECMs through the involvement of integrin β5 and FCHo2 as already reported by Cui’s lab, the manuscript should integrate the effect of the mutants of both FCHo2 and ITGβ5 cytoplasmic tail in cell migration in 3D in order to correlate their molecular findings with biological process and in particular in cancer cell invasion. The phosphomutants FCHo2 might be tested in comparison with β5 integrin mutants (comparison between mutants able or unable to interact with FCHo2 or talin or both). Moreover, considering the role of FCHo2 in soft matrix the state of phosphorylation of FCHo2 might be tested in condition of soft matrix versus stiff matrix. In other terms, the phosphorylation state of Y766 might control cell migration between stiff and soft environnement where focal adhesions and curved adhesions were respectively occuring. It would be interesting to check.

## Authors' Response to Round 1

We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive comments, which have been extremely helpful in improving the quality of our manuscript. All three reviewers highlighted the novel insights provided by our study and suggested additional experiments to strengthen our conclusions. In response, we conducted a series of new experiments, added new analyses, substantially revised the figures, and refined the text, to more accurately reflect the current state of knowledge in the field.
Since the initial review, the first author, Chih-Hao Lu, had graduated from Stanford and begun a postdoctoral position at UCSF. Despite this transition, he returned to Stanford many weekends over the past ten months to work with other team members to complete the requested experiments. This extended timeline reflects the substantial efforts required to conduct the additional studies, but we have now fully addressed all reviewer suggestions and incorporated them into a comprehensive revision of the manuscript.
Below, we provide a point-by-point response to the comments. As part of this revision, we have added a new Figure 3 (all new results, shown below, detailed in the manuscript), four new supplementary figures (all new data), and updated 2 existing figures and five supplementary figures. We trust that the newly added results, analyses, and text rephrasal now make our manuscript suitable for publication.

### Reviewer 1

Although certain technical limitations prevent the authors from providing fully definitive experimental evidence for all points raised, they have made reasonable efforts to address the concerns. Overall, I find the responses and revisions satisfactory and have no further concerns.

### Reviewer 2

This largely revised manuscript has clarified major points of criticisms and questions to which extent talin1 is contributing to the avb5 integrin activation by FCHo2 in curved adhesion. The authors took a lot of care to distinguish the talin-mediated activation mechanisms of avb5 on flat surfaces from that of the curved adhesions. The current model is compelling although some questions are still outstanding such as the particular role of the transmembrane domain of b5-integrin, or investigations on the lipid-binding preference of the F-BAR domain of FCHo2. At the current state the manuscript offers a new vision and function of avb5 integrin that is not due to classical set of adapter proteins found for other integrin-dependent adhesions. The role for Y766 of b5 to serve as a phosphorylation-mediated switch in adapter proteins is a potentially very important finding considering its potential regulation by intracellular kinase signaling. The current hypothesis provided by the authors clearly opens the field for more structural and regulatory work on this specific potentially highly relevant switch for the behavior of avb5.
